analysis.one_liner: Gives the FDA authority to regulate cigarettes, restrict tobacco advertising, and ban candy-flavored cigarettes.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill with 28 cosponsors that would have let the FDA regulate tobacco was sent to committee in March 2005 and never received a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made tobacco products subject to Food and Drug Administration oversight for the first time: manufacturers would register with the government, disclose ingredients and harmful constituents, get government approval before selling new or 'less harmful' products, and put stronger warning labels on packs. It would ban candy, fruit, and spice flavorings in cigarettes — but explicitly leave menthol alone — and let the FDA restrict how cigarettes are advertised and sold. It also contains carve-outs: Congress, not the FDA, would keep the power to ban any tobacco product outright or cut nicotine to zero, the FDA could not require a prescription to buy cigarettes, could not ban sales at any category of store, and could not set the purchase age above 18.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teens, who the bill's findings say are the main target of the roughly $12.4 billion a year the tobacco industry spends on marketing [S3]; current smokers, who would get stronger warning labels, full ingredient and smoke-constituent disclosure, and protection from 'light' and 'low tar' marketing the bill says misleads people into not quitting [S3]; and the public health system, since the bill estimates cutting youth smoking in half would save about $75 billion in health care costs [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill gives the Secretary of Health and Human Services, through the FDA, authority over the manufacture, marketing, and distribution of tobacco products, including registration, inspection, recordkeeping, and user fees [S2].
It bans cigarettes from containing characterizing flavors like strawberry, cinnamon, clove, or coffee — flavors aimed at new, often young, users — though menthol is expressly left untouched [S2].
It requires premarket approval for all new tobacco products and rigorous review of any 'modified risk' product, so companies could not market reduced-harm claims without proving them [S2].
It gives the FDA authority to restrict tobacco advertising and promotion, to revise warning labels, and to order public notification or recalls of unreasonably harmful products [S2].
Manufacturers would have to disclose all ingredients, nicotine content, and harmful smoke constituents by brand, with an annually published list in plain language for consumers [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers, who would pay user fees and absorb the cost of registration, inspections, ingredient disclosure, premarket applications, and advertising limits — costs they could pass on to adult smokers through higher prices [S2]. Menthol smokers, who are disproportionately Black Americans, would keep smoking a product the bill deliberately declines to restrict [S2]. Anyone who values the current marketing practices the bill's findings say the industry spent over $12.4 billion on in 2002 would lose that channel [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Tobacco makers and, via prices, smokers

drawbacks.text: The bill explicitly preserves menthol — the one flavor still linked to a large share of youth initiation and used disproportionately by Black smokers — while banning candy and fruit flavors [S2].

Congress reserves to itself the power to ban any tobacco product or reduce nicotine to zero, so the regulator could never take either of the two most drastic public health steps without new legislation [S2].
The bill caps the legal purchase age at 18, forbids requiring a prescription, and forbids banning sales in any category of retail store, limiting how far the FDA could restrict access [S2].

An honest supporter would concede the structure is favorable to the largest manufacturer: premarket approval, user fees, and advertising restrictions fall on the whole industry and raise the cost of entering or growing a brand, and the biggest cigarette maker publicly supported FDA regulation. Critics argued this locks incumbent market shares in place even as it regulates them.

Strict limits on advertising raise a First Amendment question the bill itself spends pages defending, and critics warned that heavy restrictions could push sales into illicit trade, which the bill's own findings link to organized crime [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health upside is large — the bill's own findings cite 400,000 deaths a year from tobacco and estimate cutting youth smoking in half would save over $75 billion in health care costs [S3]. The main honest criticisms are that the menthol carve-out and the reservation to Congress of a product ban and zero-nicotine authority blunt the bill's strongest tools [S2], and that its structure burdens small and new manufacturers more than the dominant one. On balance it is a real public health gain with significant carve-outs shaped to keep the largest companies whole.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in March 2005, referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day, and sat there for the rest of the two-year Congress — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, ever [S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Mike DeWine introduced S. 666 on March 17, 2005, with 15 original cosponsors from both parties, including Ted Kennedy, Richard Lugar, Tom Harkin, John McCain, John Cornyn, and Arlen Specter [S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
Twenty-eight senators — 19 Democrats and 9 Republicans — cosponsored the bill [S4].
The action history shows no further action of any kind for the remainder of the 109th Congress: no committee hearing, no markup, no vote, and it never came to the Senate floor [S5].
A substantially similar bill eventually became law in 2009, meaning cigarette makers operated without FDA regulation for roughly four more years than this bill would have allowed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The major tobacco manufacturers came out ahead: they went on selling and marketing without FDA regulation for another four years, until a later Congress passed a version of this bill. Because the bill never became law, no candy-flavor ban, no premarket review, and no advertising restrictions took effect during this period.

for.name: Sen. Mike DeWine
for.role: U.S. Senator from Ohio; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced S. 666 on March 17, 2005 and delivered introductory remarks [S5].

for.name: Sen. Edward Kennedy and Sen. Richard Lugar
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction, giving the bill bipartisan leadership [S3].

for.name: Public health groups (Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids, American Cancer Society, American Heart Association)
for.what_they_did: Publicly championed FDA regulation of tobacco as their top legislative priority.

against.name: HELP Committee leadership under Chairman Michael Enzi
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on March 17, 2005; the record shows no hearing, no markup, and no committee vote was ever scheduled for it [S5].

against.name: Senate leadership under Majority Leader Bill Frist
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; no motion to proceed or floor debate appears in the action history [S5].

against.name: Smaller tobacco manufacturers (R.J. Reynolds, Lorillard)
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against FDA tobacco regulation, arguing it was a deal favorable to their larger rival Philip Morris.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from day one — 28 cosponsors split 19 Democrats and 9 Republicans, with conservatives like John Cornyn and moderates like Olympia Snowe on the same list [S4] — and the obstruction, if it had a partisan shape, came from committee and floor leadership rather than from a recorded vote, since no vote ever happened [S5].

industries.note: The bill would impose registration, ingredient disclosure, premarket approval, user fees, and advertising limits on cigarette makers — a heavy burden — while locking the largest incumbents in place: new products need government approval, entry costs rise, and menthol is protected. The biggest manufacturer's public support for FDA regulation reflected exactly this trade of regulation for a permanent, regulated oligopoly.

The bill bans candy, fruit, and spice flavorings but expressly preserves menthol, shielding the menthol-heavy brands from the bill's key flavor restriction while menthol remains a major on-ramp for new, often young, smokers [S2].

industries.industry: Flavored and novelty tobacco product makers
industries.note: A outright ban on characterizing flavors like strawberry, clove, cocoa, and coffee in cigarettes would eliminate their product lines, which are aimed at new users [S2].

The bill expressly excludes tobacco leaf, growers, warehouses, and grower cooperatives from FDA authority — FDA officers cannot even enter a tobacco farm without written consent — and leaves the Agriculture Department's authority over growing untouched [S3].

industries.industry: Tobacco advertising, sports sponsorship, and promotional media
industries.note: The FDA could restrict advertising and promotion to the full extent the First Amendment allows, and the bill's findings document heavy industry spending on sports sponsorship and marketing aimed at young people, so restriction would shrink this revenue channel [S2].
